What Is a Forest Worth?

Coal, compensation and the Hasdeo Arand forest of Chhattisgarh
Development versus Environmental Sustainability: The Case of Mining in India
Gopikrishnan Annamalai & Krishang Worah · 16 November 2026
Hasdeo Arand forest, Chhattisgarh

Part I02 · The case
The case

A forest that sits on top of five billion tonnes of coal

Hasdeo Arand is one of the largest unbroken stretches of dense forest in central India, covering about 1,70,000 hectares of northern Chhattisgarh.

It is home to Gond, Oraon and other Adivasi communities, it feeds the Hasdeo river, and it lies beside the Lemru Elephant Reserve.

Beneath it lie 23 coal blocks. Rajasthan’s state power utility, RVUNL, holds three of them (PEKB, Parsa and Kente Extension), and the Adani group mines them as Mine Developer and Operator.

The central question

Should India mine coal beneath one of its densest forests to power its growth, and if it does, can that loss ever be truly compensated?

A boy looks across the PEKB open-cast mine, Hasdeo Arand
Fifteen years of approvals and pushback
ApprovalCheck or challenge
2009–10
The government’s own go/no-go exercise classes Hasdeo Arand as a no-go area.
2011
The Environment Minister overrules his Forest Advisory Committee and clears the first blocks.
2014
The National Green Tribunal sets aside the PEKB forest clearance.
2021
Two expert reports disagree. Parsa is cleared on the more permissive one.
2022
The Chhattisgarh Assembly unanimously asks the Centre to cancel every Hasdeo block.
2024
The state Scheduled Tribes Commission finds that village consent for Parsa was forged.
2026
Kente Extension is cleared: 1,742.6 ha of forest and about 4.48 lakh trees.

Part I04 · The established view
The established view · Neoclassical economics

Price the forest, and mine if the gains outweigh the losses

Neoclassical economics treats nature as capital with a price. If the benefits of coal exceed the value of the forest, and the losers could be compensated, mining is the efficient choice.

74%+of India’s electricity is generated from coal.
4,340 MWof Rajasthan’s state power plants rely on these coal blocks.
The economic ideaHow India wrote it into law
Pigou 1920
Make the polluter pay for the harm it causes.
→
Net Present Value (NPV)
Miners pay up to ₹15.96 lakh per hectare for the forest’s lost services.
Kaldor–Hicks 1939
A project is efficient if the winners could compensate the losers.
→
Clearance appraisal
Forest and environmental clearances weigh a project’s benefits against its costs.
Hartwick 1977
Reinvest resource income so future generations are no poorer.
→
DMF and CAMPA
A share of royalties funds mining districts, and payments fund new forests elsewhere.
SourcesPIB, Ministry of Coal (4 Apr 2025); Ashok Gehlot’s letter, via Swarajya (2022); MoEFCC NPV revision, via The Hitavada (21 Jan 2022); Pigou (1920); Kaldor (1939); Hicks (1939); Hartwick (1977).

Part I05 · Where it strains
Where the established view strains

A coherent framework that struggles on its own terms

The established view is rational, and India has built real institutions on it. But each of its promises can be tested against the evidence from Hasdeo.

01

Is the price right?

NPV rates stayed frozen for about 13 years, and in 2022 a Supreme Court-appointed committee called the method outdated.

02

Is the money spent?

Roughly half of the ₹1.2 lakh crore collected for District Mineral Foundations is still unspent, and a CAG audit found that only 61% of afforestation funds released in 2009–12 were used.

03

Can the forest be replaced?

The government’s own Wildlife Institute of India advised against new mines, warning that harm to wide-ranging animals such as elephants can seldom be mitigated.

If the price, the payment and the replacement are all in doubt, a deeper question follows: who decides what a forest is worth? That is where the heterodox view begins.

Part II06 · The heterodox view
Heterodox critiques · I

The land is taken, but its people are left at the margins

Heterodox economics begins with a different question: not what the forest costs, but who bears the cost and how that loss is made to look fair.

Critique 1

Dispossession without proletarianisation

Sanyal (2007); Bardhan (2018)
The idea

Capital-intensive mining separates people from their land without employing them, pushing them into an informal “need economy” outside capital’s main circuit.

At Hasdeo

Diverting dense forest for PEKB cuts Adivasi households off from forests that supply an estimated 60–70% of their income, and promised jobs remain disputed.

Critique 2

Accumulation by encroachment

Pattnaik & Pattnaik (2021)
The idea

Capital takes over natural commons and uses state power to squeeze the incomes of primary producers, so that raw materials stay cheap.

At Hasdeo

About 3,700 ha has been approved for diversion since 2022, and in 2016 the state cancelled Ghatbarra village’s community forest rights.

Critique 3

Welfarist governmentality

Sanyal (2007)
The idea

The state and corporations manage displaced people through welfare schemes that legitimise extraction and quieten resistance.

At Hasdeo

DMF funds and corporate community schemes present mining as development, even while roughly half of DMF money lies unspent.

SourcesSanyal, Rethinking Capitalist Development (2007); Bardhan (2018); Pattnaik & Pattnaik (2021); ICFRE–WII study, via Hindustan Times (20 Sep 2021); Hindustan Times (28 Apr 2022); Swarajya (2026); Business Standard (16 Feb 2016); IMPRI (Dec 2025).
Part II07 · The heterodox view
Heterodox critiques · II

A forest is not a list of priced parts, and the parties are not equals

Two further critiques question how the established view sees nature, and whose power shapes the outcome.

Critique 4

Open systems and the limits of valuation

Lawson (2006); Dequech (2007); Martinez-Alier (2002); Kapp (1950)
The idea

Mainstream models treat the economy as a closed system of isolated, predictable parts. Heterodox ontology sees ecological reality as open, dynamic and interconnected, so it rejects weak sustainability: some values, such as sacred groves, elephant corridors and a way of life, cannot be expressed in money.

At Hasdeo

NPV and CAMPA price trees and hectares one at a time, but they ignore how the forest, the river, the elephants and people’s livelihoods depend on one another. A payment can legitimise a loss it does not measure.

Critique 5

Class analysis and power asymmetry

Dequech (2007); Wolff & Resnick (2012); Mearman et al. (2023)
The idea

Marxian analysis asks who produces the surplus, who takes it, and who is subordinated. Forest loss is shaped by economic, political, cultural and natural forces together, not by prices alone.

At Hasdeo

Under the Mine Developer and Operator model, a public utility holds the block while a private firm mines it: Adani Enterprises owns 74% of the PEKB operating company. Against this state–corporate alliance, villages have struggled to be heard, from the 2011 ministerial override to the forged consent at Parsa.

SourcesLawson (2006); Dequech (2007), JPKE 30(2); Martinez-Alier, The Environmentalism of the Poor (2002); Kapp (1950); Wolff & Resnick (2012); Mearman, Berger & Guizzo (2023); WII report (2021); CARE Ratings (Dec 2024); Mongabay India (28 Nov 2024).
A Gram Sabha (village assembly) meets under a tree. The forum the Forest Rights Act and PESA make central to decisions on forest land.
Part II08 · Alternatives
Alternatives and the new understanding

From pricing the forest to empowering the people who live in it

The heterodox critiques point to four changes in how mining decisions are made.

1

Human capabilitiesSen (2000); Sanyal (2007)

Move beyond numerical valuation and expand people’s real freedoms: health, entitlement to forest resources and a voice in decisions, including Community Forest Resource rights under the Forest Rights Act, 2006.

2

Self-governance and binding consent

Follow indigenous standards, and make Gram Sabha consent under PESA (1996) and the Forest Rights Act binding before any mining decision affecting a village.

3

Strong sustainability rules

Set strict rules for mining, including critical minerals, respect the boundaries of no-go zones, and keep a check on amendments such as the MMDR Amendment Act, 2025.

4

Economic support over CSR

Guarantee communities basic economic rights, spend DMF funds effectively, and combine state-led investment in irrigation and restoration with real corporate support and extension services.

The established view asks
“What is the right price for this forest?”
The heterodox view asks
“Who decides, who gains, who loses, and can this loss be priced at all?”
SourcesSen, Development as Freedom (2000); Sanyal (2007); PESA Act (1996); Forest Rights Act (2006); MMDR Amendment Act (2025); iFOREST, DMF review (Mar 2025).
